title: Il Penseroso: title and design
short: 'The pensive (contemplative) man'; the companion to L'Allegro, beginning with the same ten-line banishing prelude.
body: Milton's 'Penseroso' is his own form of Italian pensieroso, 'thoughtful, pensive'. The poem mirrors L'Allegro point for point: an exorcism in alternating six- and ten-syllable lines (rhymed abbacddeec), an invocation with a genealogy, a train of attendant personifications, a sequence of pleasures through a night and the following day, and a conditional close. Here the 'joyes' of folly are banished as L'Allegro banished Melancholy, but the melancholy now welcomed is not the disease of black bile; it is the Renaissance melancholy of scholars and seers, which Ficino, drawing on the pseudo-Aristotelian Problemata 30.1, linked with genius and Saturn. The poem is also four and twenty lines longer than its companion, and many readers think it the culmination of the pair.

title: divinest Melancholy
short: Melancholy as a goddess of wisdom: the Renaissance idea, from Ficino and the Problemata, that the melancholy temperament marks genius.
body: The ancient question why outstanding men in philosophy, politics and poetry are melancholic (pseudo-Aristotle, Problemata 30.1) was revived by Marsilio Ficino's De vita (1489), which linked the melancholy temperament and the planet Saturn with contemplation and inspired insight. Klibansky, Panofsky and Saxl trace this 'noble' melancholy through Dürer's Melencolia I. Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1621) prefaced its later editions with a poem alternating the pains and joys of melancholy, often compared with Milton's pair. Milton's goddess is 'sage and holy', a figure of religious contemplation rather than mere sadness.

title: too bright ... Black
short: Melancholy's face is so bright that it must be veiled in black for human eyes; darkness here conceals excessive light.
body: The paradox is Neoplatonic and biblical: the divine is too dazzling to be seen directly and appears to human sight as darkness (compare Exodus 33:20 and Paradise Lost 3.380, 'Dark with excessive bright'). 'Ore laid' means overlaid, and 'staid' (l. 16) means sober, steady. Black becomes the colour of wisdom, not of gloom, and the following lines justify it with examples of black beauty.

title: Prince Memnon's sister
short: Memnon, son of the Dawn and king of the Ethiopians, was famed for beauty; his sister, named Himera in Dictys Cretensis, would share it.
body: Memnon fought for Troy and was killed by Akhilleus; Odysseus says he saw no handsomer man than Eurypylus except Memnon himself (Odyssey 11.522). Classical literature hardly mentions a sister: Osgood notes that commentators found only a Himera (or Hemera) in the late Latin Troy history ascribed to Dictys Cretensis, which does not mention her beauty. Milton infers her looks from her brother's. As an Ethiopian she is a type of dark beauty, justifying the goddess's black visage.

title: That Starr'd Ethiope Queen
short: Cassiopeia, queen of Ethiopia, who offended the Nereids by her boast and was set among the stars as a constellation.
body: In Apollodorus (2.4.3) Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter Andromeda was fairer than the Nereids, and was punished by a sea monster and later placed among the stars; other classical accounts make the boast about her own beauty. Milton follows the second version, which keeps attention on dark female beauty. 'Starr'd' means turned into a constellation, and 'their powers offended' means she angered the sea deities' divine power.

title: Vesta and Saturn as parents
short: Melancholy is the child of Saturn (planet of melancholy and contemplation) and his own daughter Vesta (goddess of the chaste hearth), Milton's invented pedigree.
body: No ancient source gives Melancholy this descent. Saturn (Cronos) was the planet of the melancholic temperament and of solitary study, and ruled the golden age before Jove deposed him. Vesta (Hestia), virgin goddess of the hearth, was his daughter (Hesiod, Theogony 453-54). Milton admits the incest and excuses it as belonging to an age before such 'mixture' was 'held a stain' (l. 26). Critics read the union as joining solitude, fixity and contemplation (Saturn) with purity and steady inner fire (Vesta). 'Ida' (l. 29) is the Cretan mountain where the infant Jove was hidden, so the lovers meet before 'fear of Jove'.

title: pensive Nun ... darkest grain ... Cipres Lawn
short: Melancholy pictured as a nun in a dark dyed robe and a black stole of fine crape.
body: The nun is a figure of devotion, not a Catholic polemic point. 'Grain' meant a fast dye (originally scarlet kermes, 'grain'), so 'darkest grain' is the deepest dyed colour, perhaps dark purple. 'Cipres Lawn' (cypress or cyprus) was a fine transparent black crape, used for mourning. 'Decent' keeps its Latin sense, decens, 'comely, becoming'. 'Wonted state' (l. 37) is her customary stately bearing, and 'musing gate' her contemplative gait.

title: Forget thy self to Marble
short: Rapt in contemplation, the goddess becomes still as a statue, then fixes her eyes on the earth with a 'sad Leaden' gaze.
body: 'Commercing with the skies' means communing, holding converse with heaven. Ecstatic contemplation suspends bodily life so that the soul seems to sit in the eyes. Milton had used a similar petrifaction in 'On Shakespear' (1630), where readers are made 'Marble with too much conceaving'. Lead is the metal of Saturn, so the 'Leaden downward cast' is astrologically exact; 'sad' still carries its older sense of grave, steadfast.

title: Spare Fast and the Muses' ring
short: Fasting as the discipline that brings the poet near the gods and lets him hear the Muses singing round Jove's altar.
body: Milton's Elegy 6 (1629) tells Diodati that the poet who sings of gods and heroes must live sparingly, like Pythagoras, on simple food and water. Here Fast 'diets' with the gods, and hears the Muses who dance round the altar of Zeus at the opening of Hesiod's Theogony (ll. 1-10). The asceticism links poetic and religious vocation, a theme of Milton's early career.

title: The Cherub Contemplation
short: Contemplation imagined as one of the cherubim who guide God's fiery-wheeled chariot-throne in Ezekiel's vision.
body: Ezekiel 1 and 10 describe cherubim moving with wheels full of fire beneath the throne of God, and Milton draws on this chariot again for the Son's 'Chariot of Paternal Deitie' in Paradise Lost 6.749-59. In the angelic hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the cherubim were the order distinguished by knowledge and contemplation, so the identification is precise. Contemplation 'soars on golden wing', the highest member of Melancholy's train. 'Hist along' (l. 55) means bring along with a whispered 'hist!', in silence.

title: Philomel, the nightingale
short: Silence is to be kept unless the nightingale sings; Philomela was changed into that bird after her rape by Tereus.
body: In Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.424-674, Philomela is raped and mutilated by her sister's husband Tereus; in the end the sisters become birds, and the tradition made Philomela the nightingale. Her song is 'sweetest, saddest', the melancholy music of the night, matching the lark of L'Allegro. 'Plight' means condition. 'Most musical, most melancholy' (l. 62) was quoted and criticised by Coleridge in 'The Nightingale' (1798), who objected that nothing in nature is melancholy, though he conceded Milton's line was spoken in character.

title: Cynthia's Dragon yoke
short: The moon goddess slows her chariot to listen; Milton gives her the dragons that classical poets gave to Ceres or Medea.
body: Cynthia is Diana as moon goddess (from Mount Cynthus on Delos). In classical poetry dragons draw the chariots of Ceres and Medea (Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.642, 7.220-37), not the moon's, which usually has horses or oxen; Osgood collects the parallels. The 'accustom'd Oke' is the oak tree over which she habitually passes, perhaps with a glance at the oak sacred to Jove. 'Checks' means reins in.

title: Curfeu
short: The evening bell (French couvre-feu, 'cover fire') heard across water, swinging slow with a sullen roar.
body: The curfew bell, rung at dusk, originally signalled that hearth fires were to be covered for the night (Old French cuevrefeu). A 'Plat' is a plot of ground. Milton renders the sound by onomatopoeia and slow monosyllables: 'Swinging slow with sullen roar'. Gray's Elegy opens with the same bell, 'The Curfew tolls the knell of parting day', and Gray's poem is steeped in Il Penseroso.

title: the Lamp in the high lonely Tower
short: The archetypal image of the solitary scholar reading all night in a tower, studying 'out' the never-setting Great Bear.
body: The Great Bear never sets in northern latitudes, so to 'out-watch the Bear' is to stay awake reading until dawn hides it. The lighted tower window became an emblem of visionary scholarship: Yeats, in 'The Phases of the Moon' (1919), recalls the tower where 'Milton's Platonist / Sat late'.

title: thrice great Hermes
short: Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage to whom the Hermetic writings on God, the soul and the cosmos were ascribed.
body: The Corpus Hermeticum, translated into Latin by Marsilio Ficino (completed 1463, printed 1471), was believed to preserve the wisdom of an Egyptian priest-philosopher older than Moses, whose name means 'thrice-greatest Hermes'. Isaac Casaubon showed in 1614 that the texts were late antique, but Hermetic thought remained influential among Platonists and occultists. Pairing Hermes with Plato places the scholar's reading in the Neoplatonic tradition of the soul's ascent.

title: unsphear the spirit of Plato
short: Call down Plato's soul from the heavenly sphere where it now dwells, to explain where immortal souls go after death.
body: To 'unsphear' (Milton's coinage, OED) is to draw a spirit out of its celestial sphere. In the Timaeus (41d-42b) each soul is assigned a star to which the virtuous return; the Phaedo argues the soul's immortality. The questions asked, 'What Worlds, or what vast Regions hold / The immortal mind' when it has left 'this fleshly nook', are those of the Phaedo and the myth of Er (Republic 10). 'Mansion' means dwelling-place.

title: Daemons of the four elements
short: The Neoplatonic spirits that inhabit fire, air, water and earth, each in sympathy with a planet or element.
body: Late Platonists (Proclus, Psellus) and Renaissance occult philosophers such as Ficino and Cornelius Agrippa (De occulta philosophia, 1533) classified daemons, intermediate spirits between gods and men, by the element they inhabit. 'Consent' means sympathy or harmony (Latin consentire): the spirits' powers correspond with the planets and elements. The word 'daemon' carries the Greek sense, a spirit not necessarily evil, unlike the Christian 'demon'. Such lore was learned rather than popular, the scholar's equivalent of the fairy tales told by the fire in L'Allegro 100-114.

title: Gorgeous Tragedy: Thebes, Pelops' line, Troy
short: Greek tragedy personified, presenting the three great tragic cycles; the 'Buskind stage' is the tragic theatre.
body: Tragedy enters in a royal pall (robe) with a sceptre. Thebes means the story of Oedipus and his children (Sophocles, Aeschylus' Seven against Thebes); 'Pelops line' is the house of Atreus, Agamemnon and Orestes (Aeschylus' Oresteia); 'the tale of Troy divine' covers plays like Euripides' Trojan Women. The buskin (cothurnus), the high boot of the tragic actor, stands for tragedy as the sock stood for comedy in L'Allegro 132. 'What (though rare) of later age' grudgingly admits a few modern tragedies; editors suppose Shakespeare's among them.

title: Musaeus and Orpheus
short: Musaeus, mythical singer and pupil of Orpheus; Orpheus's song drew 'Iron tears' from Pluto and won back Eurydice.
body: Musaeus was a legendary pre-Homeric poet, often called the pupil or son of Orpheus; Virgil places him at the centre of the blessed throng in Elysium (Aeneid 6.667). His 'bower' is that Elysian dwelling. 'Iron tears' are the tears of the iron-hearted god of the dead, an oxymoron. Where L'Allegro imagined music that would have freed Eurydice completely, the pensive man recalls only that Hell granted 'what Love did seek', leaving the failure unspoken.

title: Cambuscan and Chaucer's Squire's Tale
short: Chaucer, 'him that left half told' the Squire's Tale of the Tartar king Cambuscan and his magic gifts.
body: Chaucer's Squire's Tale breaks off unfinished. It tells of Cambyuskan, king of Tartary, his sons Algarsyf and Cambalo, and daughter Canacee, and of the gifts brought to his court: a horse of brass that flies anywhere, a mirror revealing treachery, a ring by which Canacee understands birds, and a healing sword. Milton's 'who had Canace to wife' refers to Chaucer's promise to tell of a suitor who must fight for her. Spenser completed the story in Faerie Queene IV.ii-iii (Cambell and Canacee). The choice shows Milton's reverence for Chaucer as a serious, half-allegorical poet.

title: more is meant then meets the ear
short: Allegorical romance, especially Spenser's, where the story conceals a further, moral or spiritual sense.
body: 'Great Bards beside' are the romance poets, above all Spenser, and also Tasso and Ariosto, whose tourneys, trophies, forests and enchantments carry hidden meanings. Spenser's Letter to Raleigh calls The Faerie Queene a 'continued Allegory, or darke conceit'. The line has become proverbial. 'Then' is the old spelling of 'than'. Milton's later remark in Areopagitica (1644) calling Spenser a better teacher than Scotus or Aquinas shows the same view of allegory as moral instruction.

title: civil-suited Morn and the Attick Boy
short: Dawn dressed soberly like a citizen, not tricked out as when she went hunting with her beloved Cephalus.
body: 'Civil-suited' means plainly dressed like a townsman, as opposed to a courtier. 'Trickt and frounc't' means adorned and with frizzled, curled hair. The 'Attick Boy' is Cephalus of Athens, the hunter loved and abducted by Aurora (Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.700-13). 'Cherchef't' means wearing a kerchief, here a cloud. 'Minute drops' (l. 130) may mean tiny drops or drops falling at intervals of a minute; editors are divided, and both suit the after-storm stillness.

title: Cloisters, storied Windows, dimm religious light
short: The pensive man in a Gothic church or college chapel, with stained glass, organ and choir, carried to ecstasy by sacred music.
body: 'Pale' means enclosure. 'Embowed' means vaulted; 'antick' means ancient (and perhaps carved with grotesque ornament); 'massy proof' means massive and strong. 'Storied Windows' tell Bible stories in stained glass. The passage, celebrating organ, choir and anthems, has struck readers as surprising from the later Puritan pamphleteer, and some critics relate it to the Laudian 'beauty of holiness' of the 1630s; others note that Milton's father was a composer of church music and that Milton loved the organ. 'Dissolve me into extasies' describes rapture in which the soul leaves the body.

anchor: The Hairy Gown and Mossy Cell
title: the peaceful hermitage
short: In old age the pensive man hopes to become a hermit, studying stars and herbs until experience grows into prophecy.
body: The hermit in a hair-shirt ('Hairy Gown') and moss-covered cell is a romance figure, like Spenser's hermit Contemplation in Faerie Queene I.x. 'Spell' means to study, decipher letter by letter. Studying 'every Star' and 'every Herb' is natural philosophy and medicine, and in Renaissance thought such knowledge could rise to prophecy. 'Old experience' attaining 'something like prophetic strain' (song, utterance) suggests the poet-prophet Milton aspired to become.

title: The conditional close
short: Mirrors the close of L'Allegro and Marlowe's 'Passionate Shepherd': the speaker chooses to live with Melancholy.
body: The final couplet repeats the structure of L'Allegro 151-52, so the two poems end as alternative answers to the same invitation. Here the verb is 'choose', which some critics take as a sign that Il Penseroso represents the deliberate, higher choice; others note that both endings are conditional and that the poems are balanced rather than ranked. Handel's oratorio L'Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato (1740), with a third part added by Charles Jennens, shows the eighteenth century's wish to reconcile them.
